topics.title: Doppler Modes in Echo
topics.frontClue: PW knows where but aliases; CW handles speed but cannot tell where
topics.corePiece: Doppler measures blood velocity from the frequency shift: shift equals 2 times transmitted frequency times velocity times the cosine of the angle, divided by propagation speed. In echo, the beam is aligned as parallel to flow as possible and no angle correction is used, because errors over about 20 degrees significantly underestimate velocity. Pulsed wave Doppler uses one crystal to transmit and receive from a chosen depth, giving range resolution, but it aliases when the shift exceeds the Nyquist limit, half the PRF. Continuous wave Doppler uses separate transmitting and receiving elements and measures very high velocities without aliasing, but it has range ambiguity, recording the highest velocity anywhere along the beam; it is used for AS, MR, TR, AR and VSD jets. High PRF Doppler uses multiple sample volumes to raise the measurable velocity at the cost of range ambiguity. Color Doppler uses autocorrelation to show mean velocity and direction, conventionally red toward and blue away from the transducer, with variance showing turbulence.
topics.whyLock: Aliasing is the classic question. To reduce it, raise the scale or PRF, shift the baseline, use a lower transmit frequency, reduce depth or switch to CW Doppler. Trap: increasing the transducer frequency makes aliasing worse because the shift increases. Trap two: CW cannot localize a jet, so a high velocity could be AS, MR or something else along the line; use timing, shape and the 2D image to identify it. Color jets depend on gain, Nyquist limit and frame rate; a lower Nyquist limit makes jets look larger, so standard settings around 50 to 70 cm/s are used for regurgitation.

topics.title: M-Mode & Tissue Doppler
topics.frontClue: M-mode is motion over time at one line; tissue Doppler hears the slow, loud myocardium
topics.corePiece: M-mode displays the motion of structures along a single scan line over time, with very high temporal resolution because thousands of pulses per second are sent down one line. It is ideal for timing events and fast motion: valve opening and closing, SAM, aortic valve notching in HCM, mitral fluttering in AR, RV collapse in tamponade, and TAPSE. Color M-mode of mitral inflow measures flow propagation velocity, with values above about 50 cm/s considered normal. Tissue Doppler imaging measures myocardial velocities, which are low velocity and high amplitude, the opposite of blood; the wall filter and gain are reduced to display them. PW tissue Doppler at the mitral annulus records s', e' and a'. Normal e' is at least about 7 cm/s at the septal and 10 cm/s at the lateral annulus. Strain and strain rate describe deformation; global longitudinal strain more negative than about -18 percent is generally normal.
topics.whyLock: M-mode is a timing tool; when a question asks about rapid events or precise timing, it is often the answer. Trap: an oblique M-mode cursor overestimates LV dimensions, so 2D linear measurements are now preferred. Tissue Doppler, like all Doppler, is angle dependent, so annular velocities are taken from apical views where motion is parallel to the beam. Strain from speckle tracking is relatively angle independent but vendor dependent, so serial studies should use the same platform. Remember that tissue Doppler filters are the reverse of blood flow Doppler: reject low amplitude, keep low velocity.

topics.title: Harmonics, Artifacts & ALARA
topics.frontClue: Harmonics clean the picture, artifacts fake structures, ALARA keeps exposure low
topics.corePiece: Tissue harmonic imaging receives echoes at twice the transmitted frequency, which are generated as sound propagates nonlinearly through tissue. Harmonics form mostly in the central beam and deeper tissue, so they reduce near-field clutter, side lobe and reverberation artifacts, improving endocardial border definition, particularly in difficult patients. Pulse inversion is a common method. A drawback is that valves and walls look thicker. Common echo artifacts include reverberation, parallel lines behind strong reflectors such as prosthetic valves or calcium; acoustic shadowing behind mechanical valves and calcification; side lobe and grating lobe artifacts, which place false echoes in the aortic root or LA; mirror image artifacts, duplicating structures across a strong reflector such as the pericardium; refraction, causing side-by-side duplication; near-field clutter mimicking apical thrombus; and range ambiguity. Safety follows ALARA: as low as reasonably achievable output and exposure time. The mechanical index reflects cavitation risk, with an FDA limit of 1.9 for most diagnostic applications, and the thermal index reflects heating. TEE probes monitor tip temperature.
topics.whyLock: Artifacts are tested by asking how to tell a real structure from a false one. Real structures appear in more than one view, have anatomic attachments and move independently; artifacts often sit at fixed multiples of a reflector's depth or move with it. Trap: harmonics improve borders but thicken valves, so do not diagnose valve thickening from harmonic images alone. Trap two: increasing gain does not fix shadowing; change the window. For ALARA, reduce output power before increasing receiver gain, and freeze the image when not scanning. Low MI settings are used for contrast to avoid bubble destruction.

topics.title: Contrast & Agitated Saline
topics.frontClue: Commercial microbubbles cross the lungs; agitated saline bubbles do not
topics.corePiece: Ultrasound enhancing agents are gas-filled microspheres, such as perflutren lipid or protein microspheres and sulfur hexafluoride microbubbles, small enough to pass through the pulmonary capillaries and opacify the left heart. ASE recommends contrast when two or more contiguous LV segments are not visualized, to improve EF and wall motion assessment, detect LV thrombus, confirm apical HCM, LV noncompaction or aneurysm and assess masses. Imaging uses a low mechanical index, about 0.2 or less, to avoid destroying bubbles. Agitated saline, mixed with a small amount of air and sometimes blood, produces larger bubbles that are filtered by the lungs, so it normally opacifies only the right heart. It is used to detect intracardiac shunts such as PFO and ASD, often with Valsalva release or cough, and to enhance TR Doppler signals. Bubbles in the left heart within about three cardiac cycles suggest an intracardiac shunt, while later appearance suggests an intrapulmonary shunt. Left arm injection with early coronary sinus opacification indicates a persistent left SVC.
topics.whyLock: Know which agent does what: commercial contrast is for the left heart and endocardial borders, agitated saline for shunts and the right heart. Trap: an inadequate Valsalva or high LA pressure can mask a PFO, so release the strain once the RA is opacified to transiently raise RA pressure above LA pressure. Trap two: the timing of bubbles in the left heart distinguishes intracardiac from intrapulmonary shunting. High MI destroys bubbles and causes apical swirling, so lower the MI; swirling can also mean too little agent, while too much agent causes far-field (basal) attenuation shadowing, so adjust the infusion rate. Monitor patients during and after commercial agent administration.

topics.title: TEE Indications & Views
topics.frontClue: From the esophagus, the LA is closest; look for appendage clot, vegetations and dissection
topics.corePiece: Transesophageal echo places a high-frequency transducer in the esophagus and stomach directly behind the heart, avoiding lung and chest wall, so posterior structures such as the LA, LA appendage, mitral valve, interatrial septum and descending aorta are seen in high resolution. Common indications are excluding LA appendage thrombus before cardioversion or ablation, suspected endocarditis and abscess, prosthetic valve dysfunction, aortic dissection, cardioembolic stroke and PFO evaluation, mitral valve repair planning, intraoperative monitoring and guidance of structural interventions. Contraindications include esophageal stricture, tumor, perforation, recent esophageal surgery and active upper GI bleeding. Standard views include the midesophageal four-chamber view at about 0 degrees, the mitral commissural view at about 60 degrees, the two-chamber view at about 90 degrees, often used for the LA appendage, and the long-axis view at about 120 to 140 degrees. The midesophageal aortic valve short axis is about 30 to 45 degrees, the bicaval view about 90 to 110 degrees, and transgastric views show the LV short axis and allow Doppler alignment for aortic valve gradients.
topics.whyLock: TEE trades patient comfort and small risk for image quality, so the exam asks when it is worth it. Think posterior and small: appendage thrombus, small vegetations, prosthetic mitral regurgitation and abscesses. Trap: the distal ascending aorta and proximal arch form a blind spot because the air-filled trachea lies between the esophagus and aorta. Trap two: aortic valve gradients are often underestimated from midesophageal views; use deep transgastric views for alignment. Complications include sore throat, aspiration, esophageal injury, arrhythmias and methemoglobinemia from benzocaine spray. Patients fast and are monitored during sedation.
